subtopic: NOTICE OF MOTION RE CENSORING WITHDRAWN.

speechtext:
On the notice of motion:
Resolved, That the Rules of the House be amended by inserting the following rules immediately after Rule 24 :
Censoring the Official Report of the Debates. 24A. The Speaker of the House of Commons, of his own motion, or upon the report of the Chief Censor, may order that any adverse statement, report or opinion, concerning the causes of the present war, or the motives or purposes for which Canada or the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, or any of the allied nations, entered upon or prosecutes the same, which may tend to arouse hostile feeling, create unrest, or unsettle or inflame public opinion, or any unfavourable statement, report or opinion concerning the action of Canada, the said United Kingdom, or any allied nation, In prosecuting the war, or any statement, report or opinion, which may tend to weaken or in any way detract from the united effort of the people of Canada of the prosecution of the war, made by any Member or Members of the House of Commons, shall not be included in or shall be deleted from the official report of the Debates of the House of Commons.
24B. The Speaker of the House of Commons may, in cases where he deems it necessary, order that the printing of the official report of the Debates in the House of Commons be suspended for such time as he may fix in order to afford opportunity for the making by the Chief Censor of a report as provided for in the last-mentioned section, and the determination by the said Speaker as to whether any portion of such report should be excluded or deleted.

Bid, TO AMEND THE CIVIL, SERVICE ACT
AND TO BRINK} THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
The House again in committee on Bill No. 53, respecting the Civil Service of Canada.-Mr. Boivin in, the Chair (from May 10).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee adjourned last night we had completed the general discussion of the Bill and had begun its consideration clause by clause. Section 1 has been adopted.
On section 2-Definitions:

This is a very important Bill, and I think it should not be pressed through the House in the dying hours of the session. I believe it would be in the public interest if the Bill was left over and a committee were appointed to examine it carefully and report at the next session of the House. I firmly .believe that something should be done in, the way of Civil Service reform, but in, my opinion this Bill is altogether too drastic.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Best) was perfectly in order in discussing the action of the Civil Service Federation in reference to this Bill. I say that if the man who wrote this insulting circular to the members of this House got his just deserts he would be brought to the bar of this House. The circular is an insult to every hon. member. Talk about influence! Why, that organization is the influence that is at the bottom of the whole thing. It is a countrywide organization, and is endeavouring to force this Bill through. I think it is time the members of
r

this House took cognizance of its actions. What an insult to insinuate' that me\nbers of this House are influenced by some mysterious agency behind the scenes! The mysterious agency behind the scenes is the influences these civil servants are trying to exert, and the men who wrote that circular are after promotion for themselves; everybody knows that. I think it is high time these men were called to time. The Government .should find out whether or not these men have a right to send such an insulting circular to members of this House.
I think it was perfectly in order for my hon. friend to read the circular.
Would my hon. friend read the whole circular?
The hon. gentleman has received a copy as has everyone else.
Honi soit qui mal y pense.
Read it in full.
It is a circular of the Civil Service Federation of Canada. Ae I have your permission, Mr. Chairman, I shall read the circular.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I resent the remarks
of the hon. member as to my having called the former speaker to- order. I did not call the hon. member to order because he was discussing the circular. I called him to order because he was discussing the salaries* of postmasters in Canada, which is altogether different.	,

I suppose that comes
under another clause and we can take it up when that clause is under discussion. At the top of this circular is "The Civil /Service Federation of Canada." And at the side I find the names of the officers and a list of affiliated .organizations, as follows :
President-Walter Todd, House of Commons, Ottawa ; Vice-Presidents : Maritime Provinces- S. W. Wilkins, St John, N. B.; Quebec-H. McLaughlin, (Montreal; (Manitoba-C. A. Hives, Winnipeg; Saskatchewan-Charles Gardiner, Regina ; Alberta-A. Venables, Calgary ; British Columbia-J. E. Fagan, Vancouver ; Secretary-Treasurer-F. 'Grierson, Finance,. Ottawa, (P. O. Box 4*4) ; Assistant Secretary-Treasurer -I,. D. Burling, (Mines, Ottawa; Organizing Secretary-T. T. Hawkins, P. O. Inspector, Ottawa.
Composed of the Following Affiliated Organizations of Civil Servants.
(Dominion Postal Clerk's Association (35 branches) ; Dominion Customs Association, (20 branches) ; Railway Mail Clerk's Federation, (15 branches).
Local Organizations.
Charlottetown, Quebec, Ottawa, Perth, Sarnia, Sault Ste. Marie, Vancouver, Victoria.
Class Organizations.
Excise:	Sherbrooke, .Stratford, London,
Hamilton; Immigration: Niagara Falls, Winnipeg ; Marine: Halifax; Meat Inspectors: Toronto, (2) ; Militia: Halifax; Naval: Halifax, Esquimau; Public Works: Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg.
Then the circular goes on to say:
Dear Sir,	-
The Public .Service, performing alike in peace and war the national business, is surely one of Canada's greatest assets. We are addressing you because you are one of tha directors in Canada's business enterprises and so responsible for the results. We are addressing you at a time when events afford you the opportunity to co-operate in an. Act that will remove a serious handicap to national efficiency and so contribute to the one great aspiration of all Canada's public men,-the winning of the war.
Every one who. wants a little salary always thinks that it must be granted to him an order to win the war.
Hear, hear.

My right hon. friend knows that.
' Sir WILFRID ,LAURIER: I do.

The minister in charge of the Bill is here and he can stand up and tell the House whether there ever was any elaborate organization endeavouring to put a stop to this great measure or whether this letter is all bunkum and an attempt to coerce the members of this House into the passing of a measure without due consideration. As one member of the House I do not object to real Civil Service reform but when we have a measure of such vast consequence to the whole country and one by which we. will tie ourselves down to a lot of bureaucrats', it should -be placed before a committee of this House and threshed out for a whole session so that we would know, what we were doing. Nobody really seems to understand what the measure means. I have read this circular and I say unhesitatingly that if I were a minister of the Crown and a man in the Civil Service with whom I had anything to do wrote an. insulting letter like that to me and to members of the House I would suspend him immediately. What right has ,a man who is a servant of this House to address this House in such a contemptuous way?

I would like
to say a word1 in reply to that sweeping condemnation of the Civil Service for presuming to represent their position to their employers the members of this House and the representatives of the people. I have in my experience heard similar statements made in regard to other large bodies of employers when their employees wouto presume to represent their case to their employers as the Civil Service have done here. I do not see that it is inconsistent with the good of the public service that civil servants should be organized if they wish to be just the same ;as the servants of any other large employing body. It matters not whether they are in the em-p'oy of a large corporation or of the people of Canada. I question very much whether the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) woulld object if some one came along with a proposition that involved a large organization of capital and that was going to be the employer of a large body of men. Any one who stands up iand indulges in a sweeping condemnation of any group of men for presuming to organize and present their case to their employers is taking just the same position that a great many of the autocratic employers took a generation ago but who have been compelled to get down from that lofty pedestal. The observations made by the hon. gentleman have no reference 'whatever to the merit or genius of this Bill. The Bill is either good
['Mr. Currie.]
or bad according to its details. The object is. to take the Civil Service out of politics and to get rid of the curse of the patronage system, a principle which ought to commend it to every one. There is nothing inconsistent with the good of the public service that the men who are engaged in that service should have an honest desire for promotion. Why should not a man entering the Civil Service have the same right to want to get to the top as the man in the service of a railway company or of any other employer?
Why should he not get to the top-the Bill provides that a man in the second class can never get to the top.

Simply because some member of Parliament with sufficient pull, -whenever a position is open in the Civil Service that is worth anything, railroads some of his friends into it. That is why they cannot get to the top. The opportunity for promotion does not exist in the Civil Service as it does in any other line of business simply on account of the patronage system. If this Bill is not complete in its details this House can improve it. If we find when we have gone through it that there are some things that are incomplete, we can take it up another year and make the necessary improvements. But, the principle is the right one. The public service ought to be put upon the same ground as any other class of service.

Just a moment. I desire to answer the hon. gentleman (Mr. G. B. Nicholson), and I shall do so in a very few words. The gentleman who has sent the circular, Mr. Grierson, sits in the gallery constantly watching the proceedings of the House. He is the secretary, or occupies other official position in the Civil Service Association, and publishes the Civil Service paper, The Civilian. It is a shame-I would not for one moment stand it if I were a minister of the Crown-the abuse that ministers are handed out in every issue of that paper. When a minister tries to exercise any discipline over 'any official in his department he is subjected to a torrent of abuse from the paper published by this man, Mr. Grierson, one of the signatories to this circular. The hon. member (Mr. Nicholson) comes down here full of enthusiasm and thinks he is going to regenerate the whole world through the medium of this Bill. I do not object to a man who is selling his labour belonging to any organization, but I say that it is a danger-a danger to the country-that the official?

of Canada should be allowed to set themselves up in an organization of this kind and make these raids on the treasury. I speak as a public man, not as one who is going around looking for votes, and this organization-the very thing that has destroyed Russia- is alarming. It is a thing that is^ going to create all sorts o>f factions in this service whereby it will be nothing more than a series of disjointed units and broken links. I say that the ministers henceforth should put their foot down on these men who have the audacity to insult the House of Commons with a circular of this kind. This organization has nothing to do with the Federation of Labour, or any of the trades unions that are trying to render a service to the country in these troublesome times. It is only a short time ago since the greatest labour man on the whole of this continent stood upon the floor of this chamber and called upon everybody to perform public service. Can anyhody tell me that public service is linked up in the organization which has expressed its sentiments in this circular? The members of this or-ganizatioh are united for the purpose ot raiding the treasury and bringing pressure to hear upon members of this House and the ministers-especially the ministers- and it has been done to' the extent that a minister, as far as I can see, is only a cipher to register in has department the acts of an organization which is not responsible either to the House or the people of the country. For that reason I think the Acting Minister <_f Finance should make a statement and say whether there has been any organized movement to try and stop this Bill, or whether these men are only indulging in further misrepresentations.
I did not catch the wording of the circular. Does it give practical reasons why this Bill should be supported, or does it insinuate that the members are not doing their duty?
The circular consists of a string of insinuations from start to finish.
They say that to win the war you have got to have such a Bill.

Paragraph (a) of clause 2 of the Bill defines "Civil Service" as meaning and including:
All classes of officers, clerks and employees- and so forth-
-appointed by the Governor in Council or other competent authority before the first day of
112$
July, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two or thereafter appointed or employed in a manner provided by the Civil Service Act for the time being, in force.
Is there not a better way in which that definition could be stated? I understand that the Civil Service includes practically all the employees of the Government of Canada. In that case why limit the definition to those employed "in the manner provided by the Civil Service Act for the time being enforced" which I presume is the old Civil Service Act? Why not say that all the employees of the Government come under this Act?
,Sir WILFRID LAURIER: Hear, hear.
And all the officials.

I wish to distinguish between the . Civil Service and the Public Service.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER; What is the difference?
That is the point I want to make. Why make such a distinction when, you are going to- abolish patronage and bring all the employees under the Civil Service Commission?

There are a great number of war commissions operating today in the city of Ottawa whose employees are but temporary, and on the cessation of war these commissions will cease to exist. While the Civil Service Commission should have the right to appoint hereafter all persons employed by these war commissions, it was not deemed desirable to consider such persons as part of the Civil Service.
Are the Dominion police part of the Civil Service, and if not, why?
The Alounted Police are not part of the Civil Service.
I said Dominion Police, not North West Mounted Police.
The press gangs going round the city and country.
The Dominion Police, I think, are part of the Civil Service.
Is the minister sure? I am told they are not, and why is it so?
I asked the minister a very important question whether any organization had approached the Government with a view to stopping the passage of this Bill?

I am very sorry, hut I did not have the opportunity of

answering the question put by my hon. friend from Simeoe- I quite agree with the principle enunciated by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), but I am inclined to agree with the views expressed by the members for Dufferin and Simeoe as to the impropriety of the Civil Service bombarding members of Parliament in respect to the passage of this Bill. I have been flooded during the past week with telegrams from every part of Canada, and I have taken pains to let the officers of the organized Civil Service know that I resent the manner in which they have approached members of Parliament during the past few days by circular and by telegram. So far as I know there has been no organized effort on the part of anybody to defeat the passage of this Bill. I should like to say in connection with clause 2 that subsections a and to 'are substantially as they now appear in the present Civil Service Act. The only difference in c is that there is an addition to the officers maimed as Deputy Heads, such as the Controller of the Mounted Police, the Superintendent of Insurance, the Dominion Archivist and the assistant to the chairman and secretary to the Commission of Conservation. The purpose of making these officers deputy heads within the Act is that they control their staffs, and therefore it is necessary for the proper working of the Act to define them as deputy heads.

What is the exact meaning of clause 2? Subsection (a) defines "Civil Service" as including all classes of officers, clerks and employees. Subsection (c) defines what is meant by "deputy" or "deputy head" and so on.
I want to know whether the deputy is comprised in the Civil Service or not?
Mr. A. K. MAC'LEAN: The deputy ministers are part of the Civil Service hut they are appointed by the Governor in Council.
The deputy heads should be part of the Civil Service and they seem to come within the meaning of subsection (a). They are employees of the Government and they are in the Civil Service.
A deputy minister is an officer-
He is an officer and therefore part of the Civil Service.
He is part of the Civil Service but he is appointed by the Governor in Council.
I understand that and I do not disapprove of the appointment of deputy ministers by the Government but he is also a member of the Civil Service, and you make a special provision for him.

Section 41 of the Bill provides:
Except as herein otherwise provided, and except in the case of deputy heads, appointments to positions in the .pulblic service shall he by competitive examination,

That excludes deputy
ministers from the examination, hut not from membership in the 'Civil Service.

In the large or small
post offices, customs offices, and inland revenue offices throughout the country we have some very excellent officers in technical, clerical or official positions. Why should they not have the dignity, if there toe any dignity attached to it, of being in the Civil Service instead of being classified as the Outside Service. I understand the [DOT]object of this Bill is to change present conditions. The Civil Service is practically ilimited to Ottawa and to a few technical positions outside of Ottawa; the rest of the pulblic servants are called the Outside Service. If we are to have real Civil Service reform, men of an equal standing outside *of Ottawa should be in the Civil Service.
Hear, hear.

I refer especially- to men on the permanent staff, not those on the temporary staff, employed for a few weeks under rush conditions. My reference is to the permanent officers of the Customs, Post Office, Inland Revenue and such other departments as have permanent -officers throughout the country.
This is practically a temporary Bill?

Yes,
M,r. TURRIFF: Would it not be better to leave this Bill over until the commission report what they propose by way of amalgamating the outside and- inside services?
I think it would be a good) thing to have that done, and to have the whole service taken out of politics as far as possible and to do away with patronage. It seems to me that the Committee of the Whole is not a good body to deal with this Bill clause by clause. We have not the' time now at the end of the session to discuss it fully. If the Bill is now dealt with I venture to say there is not one member in ten-and I will be one of them-who. will understand what the Bill means when we get through. A committee should) he appointed to deal with it, such as the committee dealing with pensions, which would investigate the matter fully and report during the next session, by which time we will have the report of the Civil Service Commission. The House would then be in a position to deal with it to the satisfaction of both the Civil Service and the country. There is something in the circular sent to mem-bers^-though I do not blame the service very mnch-that I do not like, that is the .suggestion that the winning of the war depends on the passing of this Bill to suit the Civil Service. The Civil Service have no complaint to make in my judgment in connection with the war. Many of those who went to the front have been getting two salaries, and it does not become them to come before Parliament and say that the passage of this Bill is necessary to the winning of
the war. That is only a bit of buncombe.
I move that this matter-be left over until next session, and that a committee be appointed to study the matter before we deal with the Bill.
There has been lots of buncombe about the winning of the war
I rose when the hon. gentleman did to second the motion of the hon. member tor Assinibioa.
Is there ,a motion?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member please repeat the motion?
I would move that a committee be appointed to consider this Bill and make a report at the next session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have to rule the
motion out of order, as not being competent to be moved in Committee of the Whole. The only motion that could .be made by the hon. member at this istage would be that the committee rise and report progress, so that the House may deal with the question.
Mr. Chairman,-

Before my hon. friend proceeds, I would like to have an explanation from him. When my hon, friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) concluded his remarks by asking if the Bill was presented as a temporary measure only, I understood the acting minister to nod assent. I desire to know if this is a permanent measure or only a temporary. If it is .a temporary measure, I shall have something to say about it later on.

When the member for Vancouver used the word " temporary," I assumed that he did- not mean that this Bill when enacted would be but temporary; I assumed he meant it was not to be considered as a complete Bill, and that it would be subject to amendment later.
What amendment?

It will be subject to amendment later as any other Act. It. is not a temporary Bill. We must have a Civil iService Act as we have always had. I admit that the Bill may contain defects which we hope to remedy later. In answer to the member for Assiniboia I want to say that .substantially there are but eight or nine new clanses in this Bill; the whole Bill is substantially as it has been for the last ten years, and theie is no reason why the iHous-e should delay many hours in its passage.
To win the war.

Reference has been made by an horn, member to the effect that the Outside Service was to be dealt with in thi-s Bill, and I would ask whether in the reorganization and reclassification of the Outside Service it is the intention through this^ Bill to place that service on the same footing as the Inside Service as regards appointments, promotion, salaries, and superannuation.

The purpose of the Bill is to apply to the Outside Service the principle carried out in the Inside Service in the matter of appointments. Otherwise the Bill is not applicable to the Outside Service, nor is it possible to make it so until we have the report on the reorganization and classification of the Outside Service which the Civil Service Commission purposes making during the recess.

I am in favour of Civil Service reform, that is, a real reform. If the object of this legislation is to carry out what was contained in the Act of 1908, it is not a great reform, because under that Act the Government could at any moment, by Order in Council, bring the Outside Service under the Civil Service Commission. I am sure that my hon. friend knows how to handle Orders in Council; there has been *a literal manufacture of them by the Government. Why this legislation in the last days of the session, when the Government could, by Order in Council, bring the Outside Service under the Civil Service Commission?
It is true that there was such a section in the old Act, hut it was not workable.
Why?

The Civil Service Act now in force was designed to apply solely to the Inside Service. It is true that the Act gives the power to put the Outside Service under its^ operation, but it is not practicable that this be done. For instance, if an Order in Council was passed putting the Outside Service under the operation of the Civil Service Act, the salaries of the Inside Service would automatically apply to the Outside Service. The section to which my hon. friend refers was carelessly drafted; it had not sufficient consideration at the time it was passed, and it could not possibly be put into operation.

Is it not a fact that the Outside Service has been brought under the Civil Service Act by Order in Council? 
I received notice from the Government that appointments were to be made by the Civil Service Commission, and that I should have nothing to do with them. Appointments have already been made in my riding in that way.
This legislation gives statutory effect to the Order in Council.	*
An Order in Council has no statutory effect, then?
It may have the effect of a statute, but there is some doubt about it. In a case of this kind it is better to give statutory effect to the Order in Council.

This is an Act respecting the Civil Service of Canada. Clause 2, paragraph (a), defines "Civil Service" as follows:
"Civil Service" means and includes all classes of officers, clerks and employees in or under the several departments of the Executive Government of Canada and in the office of the Auditor General, etc.
Who is to control the various commissions that have been appointed? I do not see why members of such commissions should not come under the same Act as that which 'applies to the ordinary civil servant who works in a particular department.
So far as appointments are concerned, they will toe under the Civil Service Commission.

I do not see anything in this Bill that says so. Even if these commissions are only temporary, they should, unless otherwise enacted by the statute creating the commission, come under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. This would prevent the substitution of an Order in Council for Parliament, and would give members of Parliament at least a dim realization that they have a little say in. the *administration of the country's affairs. In the old Civil Service Act, as found in the Revised Statutes, the definition of "Civil Service " is practically the same as the one given here, except that the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Northwest and Yukon Territories were then excluded from its provisions,.- Later, in 1908, the definition was enlarged to include employees in Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon Territory. Between, the two another Act was passed concerning the superannuation and retirement of persons employed in the Civil Service, and in that Act " Civil Service " was

defined as- including all officers,, clerks and employees under the several departments of executive government who were paid a yearly salary and to whom the Civil Service Act applied. Included also were all such officers, clerks and employees of the second or outside division as the Governor in Council might from time to time designate; the permanent officers and servants of the Senate, the House of Commons, and the Library of Parliament; and' so on. The definition given in that Superannuation Act is a great deal broader than that given here. I do not see anything in this Bill ' which says that 'the permanent employees of the House of Commons are included in that definition. As :to the Commission, let us set out in the statute appointing them [DOT]what regulations the members and employees of them shall be subject to. If the Governor in Council appoints a commission let the officers of that commission come under the operation of the Civil Service Act. I am in favour of the principle of this Bill; I think it is right. Since we have heen in opposition we have not been overburdened with the distribution of patronage. That is a great relief, and I thank God fo^ it. Another cloud that I want to disperse, another glory that I want to put into its proper place is the statement that this is a new thing, and that this legislation is being enacted to redeem the pledges made duiing the elections by Union candidates. We heard it said last night in this House that if the Union Government did nothing hut enact this particular legislation, a * monument should be erected to perpetuate the great good they have done to this country. Let us have no -more
camouflage. With the exception of the heads, let all the other officials and- employees' of commissions appointed by the Governor in Couneil come under this Act.

It is things of that sort that we want to guard against. It was said last night b>

I must say I am with him heart and soul on this particular question. What the people want this Parliament to protect them against is what is commonly called graft. Graft is not caused by the appointment of a clerk at $1,000 or $2,000 a year, but graft is found, in the various contracts that are handed out, in the changes that are made and the extras that are paid on those contracts after they have been signed. The other day I called the attention of the Minister of Public Works to -a case of this

kind which happened in my own riding where, to favour a particular friend, a contract was given at a price lower than that of the lowest tenderer, and then the contractor, expecting to make up the difference by extras, received shamefully large amounts for shamefully small jobs, such as receiving $400 for turning a stone around in a wall. Why should we pass a Civil Service Act, if any minister of the Crown can come into the House with an appropriation to provide for the administration of certain things, and then attach this rider which seems very inoffensive per se, hut in the tail of which is the old venom:
Appointments for the purpose may be made without reference to the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
The Government have changed- the phraseology so that the old members will not understand it. 'The former phraseology was " notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act contained." It is things of that -sort -that we want to take precautions against. If we are going to make the appointments, one thing that the people are complaining about -and from which they want to he protected is, not so much the matter of overpaid civil servants, as the matter of over-crowded offices. If the minister will accept my suggestion, I sha-11-d-raft a little amendment for -the purpose of putting into the definition of " Civil Service," -all commissions or officers employed by commissions- appointed by the Governor -in -Council, .and into the definition o-f " Public -Service," all -commissions whose duties and jurisdiction are established by Parliament. Mr. CHiAtBOTi:	My hon. fri-efod from

You have always had
my sincere sympathy.

I think at -all times patronage has been opposed to -the best interests of the Civil Service -and has to -a large extent-, contributed to the defeats of 
many Governments in this country. After 1911, political patronage -in this city w-as -thrust upon me w-ith -a vengeance, and my life in Ottawa from 1911 to 1917 was a regular political hell on earth. Si-nce the passage of the Order in Council abolishing political patronage, my peace of mind hlas been greatly enhanced; a huge lo-ad has been taken off my shoulders, and I feel that my life has become worth living. If this legislation abolishes patronage, it will render the Civil Service more effective and efficient, and it will render to the people of this country a very valuable service.

I am sure every member of this House who is acquainted with my hon. friend (Mr. Chabot), would like to relieve him of the difficult position in which he has been placed since 1911. A political hell is about as bad a hell as one could expect. I do not, however, think that many of the members of this House from the various -parts of Canada are persecuted in the same way as the hon. member is. As this is the seat of government, one can readily understand how conditions here would be different from what they would be in other parts of the country. I want to point out that the- abolition of political patronage is not going to he accomplished 'by this legislation.
Patronage, as the people understand it, is not -affected by this Bill at all. I quite agree w-ith my hon. friend from Winnipeg -and the hon- member for Three Rivers that it -is the -expenditure of p-ublic money on public works in this country that is the kind of patronage the people of this country are desirous of abolishing. Patronage in appointments is comparatively a trifling matter, -so insignificant, in fact, that in the part o-f the country from which I co-m-e the people d-o no-t try for Government positions at all. We expect to have very little patronage -of that kind in the inland counties oi Canada. Doe-s th-e Pension Commission come under this Bill?
Mr. A. K. -MACLEAN: Yes, as to its employees.

No.

I presume that the powers o-f the Civil Service Commission are very similar to those -exercised by the Pensions 'Oommis-siion, -and if that is the case 1 must record imy opposition to having the Bill gone on with until we have a little more light on the subject. I have -always felt that commissions -can. perform a very useful service in this oo-untry provided they have -a -good imun at the hea)d<, hut if proper jurisdiction as not exercised over them they can be guilty of great -abuses. The defi-ndtionj of the powers of the commission does not, in -my opinion, -go as far -as it should. iMr. A. K. MACLEAN: That is- a matter of policy, -and has nothing whatever to d-o with, the 'Civil Service Bill.

In reply to my hon. ifriemid from Three Rivers-" Public -Service," as -used throughout this Bill means -and includes all officers, clerks or employees in the -service of the Crown or -of Parliament; so no person is omitted. Section 41 provides that -all appointments to -positions in the public service -shall be by competitive examination. There are certain other provisions empowering the commission to provide regulations for .appointments to the -Outside Service where it is not practicable to apply "this Act.

I think the hon. member . for South Oxford was quite in order in discussing on this -section, which defines " Commission," the question' whether the other commissions that -are governing half this country should not be included under this Bill. We are here defining " Civil Service " and the hon. member for South Oxford wants to know whether these various commissions are included in that definition.
-Sir SiAM HUGHES: In all countries there has been more or less difficulty in managing the Civil Service. Alexander Pope long ago referred to the matter in these lines:	,
For forms of government let fools contest, Whate'er is best administered, is best.
-Some departments of the Civil Service are administered -splendidly. Again, one branch of a department will be administered splendidly, while another branch will be badly administered; it depends upon the administrator in each case. The Civil Service in Ottawa is very fine in many respects. I deeply sympathize with the two members for Ottawa. I have had considerable experience with them. I can well remember getting a letter from one of these distinguished gentlemen requesting that such and such a person be forthwith appointed. . I passed the letter on without comment, and about a month later received another letter from the- member diemandiilg to know by what authority this particular person had been appointed. It -seems that -a certain fellow wanted to get in the service, and when he went to see the head of a department he wa-s told to get a letter from my good friend the junior member for Ottawa. He wrote a letter of introduction, knowing no more about the fellow, I suppose, than about -a stranger in the street, and the fellow got the job. Later on the other letter came wanting to know how he got appointed. It is true that sort of thing does not occur very often, hut it is an instance of the routine that is gone through. After all, it is the heads of departments who engineer the appointments nine times out of ten, hut the member of Parliament gets the blame; the member, is simply the -cat's-paw in the game. With regard to this circular, I know the two gentlemen who signed it. I was a little annoyed at receiving it. They are good fellows, hut they have -been in the service so long that, like a good many others, they think the period of leisure has arrived for them. Their talk about winning the- war and what the people of Canada want, is piffle. I think these gentlemen should not interfere with members of Parliament. If these gentlemen had furnished ns with some good reason why we should support the Bill, I would have been delighted to do it. But a sloppy thing like that circular is merely annoying.
Let us forget it.

Yes. Is this Bill going to control the appointment of senators? In the last election, a minister of the Crown is supposed to have bought off a candidate by offering him a sen-atorship. This minister was an old hand at the business, as he had done a similar thing before. In another

case, a new hand at the business was concerned. I should like to know if cases of that kind come under this Bill.
The hon. gentleman will have to renew that question .at another time.

I notice in the editorial column of the Citizen, which, I presume, is a Government organ, the following:
The Government has every reason to he displeased with the report, sent broadcast across the country, that the Civil Service Bill would be postponed till another session. The parties responsible for giving out such misleading information are apparently not anxious to see the Civil Service reformed by the abolition of patronage. Such reports tend to undermine the position of Union government; especially now that the government is undertaking^the responsibility of railway ownership on a national scale, with the Canadian Northern added to the government railway system, it is essential that political patronage should be eliminated.
Paragraph (f) says:
"Outside Service" means and includes the other officers, clerks and employees included in the public service, not being part of the Inside Service.
Then paragraph (g):
"Public Service" means and includes all officers, clerks or employees in the service of the Crown or of Parliament.
That seeems all right, but at page 13 of the Bill you exclude the railway .service. Some ihon. gentlemen, like my hon friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) fortunately have not been in contact with the Government railway system of the Dominion. They do not have any Government railways running through their parts of the country. But eventually this Government is going to take over the railway systems of Canada, including the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk Pacific, so that we will have .extensive Government ownership. If Government ownership is going to be thus extended, it is absolutely essential, if this Bill is going to be any benefit in eliminating patronage, that it- be applied to the railway service as well as to any other part of the public service. If you were in my province, where we have one mile of Government railway to every 300 inhabitants and observed the position in regard to patronage, you would *appreciate the importance of what I am trying to tell the committee. In the name of common sense, why should the railway service be eliminated from this Bill? It looks to me very suspicious. If the Government are really in earnest in their desire to give us this reform I am in favour of it.

The reason for my attitude with regard to this measure is that I have seen the system worked out in England. In the Old Country they have almost entirely done away with the curse of patronage as administered by politicians. The system has done more than that. It has enabled a man, upon entering the public service, to know that his salary and his job are going to remain with him as long as he behaves himself and that he is not subject to being fired with a change of Government. The result is that men can afford to take a less wage, and millions and millions of pounds have been saved to the people of Great Britain from the very fact that they have adopted this principle of Civil Service reform. That is what is going to happen here. A great deal of the legislation that is passed now-a-days has particular reference to war times but this measure should be framed to meet the conditions which will exist when the w.ar is over. An hon. gentleman on the other side pointed out that this was a good time for .the Union Government to do something. In the name of common sense, let it do something under this Bill because up to the present it has done nothing beyond putting the country in a state of turmoil. I would strongly urge placing the Government railway system employees under the operation of this Bill.	^ _

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the definition of "Public Service."
"Public Service" means and includes all officers, clerks or employees in the service of the Crown or of Parliament.
Are not all classes of officers, clerks or employees "employed in or under the several departments of the executive government of Canada" employees in the service of the Crown?
Yes.
Well then "Public Service" includes the whole service of the Dominion?
It includes everybody who is in the employ of the Government, or the Parliament of Canada and only excepts railway and steamship employees and lighthouse keepers, I think.
"Public Service" includes the Civil Service?
Yes.
It does, not include soldiers?
No.

But it includes every
person in the employ of the Crown. I fail to see any difference.
Let us take that section. You use "Civil Service" and "Public Service," and they mean the same thing?
The words "Public Service" are used throughout the Act. It is the better term and it includes everybody in the service.
Is there an accepted definition for the term public service?
Not other than this.
In the old Act there was a schedule to determine who were civil servants, and in the Superannuation Act they extended the definition to cover all, *whether in the Inside or Outside Serv'ce.

Have the Civil Service
(Federation of Canada, on whose letter paper this circular was written, had this ijfill before them and have they approved of it?

I cannot say
*whether they have approved of it or not. I know they had it before them and that the association made representations to the Government about certain clauses in the Bill.

What do the Government think of the federation, through their secretary and president, writing a circular to the members containing these words:
We are addressing you because you are one of the directors in Canada's business enterprises and so responsible for the results.

Yes.
It would appear from recent items in the press that some influential agency is endeavouring to dissuade the Union Government from proceeding with the Bill for Civil Service Reform by the abolition of patronage in appointments and promotion to the Public Service.

the minister share the view that the Government should be under suspicion by Mr.. Grierson that the Government has been influenced in some way in regard to the passage of the Bill? Quite true, the Bill has been on the members' files and the fact of the minister saying that it is on the files would indicate he thinks that every member should have read it. ' I have an item which I think I should bring up here with regard to appointments. I am entirely in favour of the principle of this Bill, and I am anxious to get rid of every vestige of patronage. When I was first elected to Parliament I went to the local committees and asked them to take the patronage -away from me, because I did not want it. The cry was then raised, "You will be responsible, you will have to take it yourself." Well I have had no trouble, and the matter has not bothered me. The only trouble I have had has -arisen since I came, here lately, concerning a certain ap-

pointment. A deputy undertook to recommend to a minister the appointment of a man in my county to a responsible position upon an international cheese board. The Government appointed a man who had the capacity all right, but whose son was married to a girl who had four brothers at the front. That man was out against Union Government in the riding that I represent, in South Perth, and in West Huron or North Huron.
He was a wise man.
He's all right.

The hon. member for Three Rivers says this man was wise, and another hon. gentleman says he is all right. I am not complaining, the party in question is a free man. The young woman to whom I have referred was married to this man's son, had four brothers at the front: one had been just killed, another has since been killed, the third has been wounded, and the fourth is still on active service. The husband's father and the husband both declared that the woman would never be *allowed to poll her vote. They prevented her from polling her vote as a soldier's sister, and she did not poll it. Now the appointment of that man to the position in question seared and shocked the conscience of the loyal people in the county which I represent. It seared and shocked the conscience of those who had not voted. I think it seared and shocked the conscience of a few pro-Germans, the thing was so heinous in its character. I spoke to the minister about the appointment, and he said that for his information he had depended upon his deputy.
I do not blame him, he was new in the position, but I want to fell hon. gentlemen that deputies assume powers that usurp the ordinary functions of members of parliament who ought to know about these appointments. The deputy in question might have inquired from somebody. I do not want to be consulted in such matters, but as member for the riding I do not want to be insulted, and I shall not stand for that sort of carelessness in the future, either from the Civil Service or anybody else. I think there should be some decorum displayed in connection with these matters, and some courtesy, and reasonable attention paid to the position of the member toy ministers and deputies, so that a man will not be held in contumely and contempt by things being done in his riding for which people hold him responsible, although he has had nothing to say in regard to them.

I hope the Civil Service will remember that there are duties devolving on them towards the public men of this country, and if members are not to be consulted as to who is to be appointed to positions, at least they should be consulted as to whether any Tea-son exists for not selecting .such men as I have described.

An exception was made of the employees of the Government Railway System because it was found difficult to apply the Act to that service. And the Civil Service
commissioners will, be appointed by the Crown?

Mr. A. K. MAfCLEAN: The words "public service" occur in the present Civil Service Act but they had no definition. I really do not know why they were put in. Yes.

Yes.

I -understand that, but the moment this Act passes it will .apply only to what is known as the present Inside Service, not to what is known as the Outside Service.

I am not satisfied as to the definition of " public service." If the term " public service " includes everything, we can leave out the definition " Civil Service," and I still stand by my proposition that it should be defined as follows: "Public service" means and includes all officers', clerks and employees in the service of any commission constituted by virtue of an Act of Parliament, whereby the mode of appointment, dismissal, and so on, are therein determined. That would bring the employees of the Senate and the House of Commons under the definition of Civil Service. As the definitive clause is now drawn we do not know what it means. It says:
"Civil Service" means and includes all classes of officers, clerks an.d employees in or under the several departments of the Executive Government of Canada and in the office of the Auditor General and in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, appointed hy the Governor in Council or other competent authority before .the first day of July, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two

I suppose these men might request superannuation or take advantage of any law passed by this Parliament to protect Civil servants for performing faithful duty to the country. -or thereafter appointed or employed in the manner provided in the Civil Service Act for1 the time 'being-, in force.
We do not know what employees these are, or anything about them. I would substitute for that definition the following:

I want to protest against anything which will take away from the Act, if we are going to pass it-and I am in favour of it, and think we should pass it,-the power to appoint the personnel of commissions such as the Bureau of Public Information headed by Mr. Nicholls, and other commissions which are the result of the very prolific Orders in Council we have to-day.
That is why the definition o'f "public service" was put in the Bill, to cover just such cases as my hon. friend suggests.
May I ask why the term " Civil Service " has been defined, if it covers everything?

That word rather denotes the purpose of the Bill. It is an old sedbion, and it was not considered desirable to revise entirely every section of the Act. We might very well drop the definition "Civil Service" altogether, but I do not think it would be well to do that.
Why not say that the "Civil Service" means all officers, clerks and employees in the service of the Crown or in the public service?
Except that the word "public service" is used in another sense throughout the Bill.
Why not leave "Civil Service" out and say that the "public service" means all that the former term includes?

In speaking on this matter yesterday, I expressed my inability to distinguish between "Civil Service" and "public service," and that may account for my inability to see where this section cov ered the Pensions Commission. I understand from the explanation that has been given that thiat commission would come under the term "public service."
Yes.

The Bill says:
"Public Service" means and includes all officers, clerks or employees in the service of the Crown or of Parliament
I would assume from the wording of that section that it would include the men who are in the public service across the sea at the present time.

That is military
service, not Civil Service.
I would imagine surely that that is public service.
It is public service in a sense, but strictly speaking it is military service, and there is a separate statute covering matters of that kind,

May I ask if the public service has been administered in this sense since the passing of the Order in Council on February 13? In listening to the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) relate what had taken place in his constituency, I felt that as the representative for the constituency from which I come I possibly ought to know something about conditions in that riding.

An appointment has recently been made there which, I assume, would not come under the Civil Service Act. In this appointment is suggested one of the reasons to which I attribute the breaking down of the Military Service Act. The official to whom I have reference was appointed representative of the Department of Agriculture on the Leave of Absence Board for military district No. 1, although he had stumped the constituency during the election campaign in opposition to Union Government and to the Military Service Act.

It would appear from a return respecting the staff of the Food Controller's office that the chairman of the Food Board reserves to himself the power to say anything he pleases, notwithstanding the Civil Service Commission or anything in the Civil Service Act. In an Order in Council respecting staff and salaries of the Food Board I find the following:
The minister observes that the Food Controller states that the above method1 of using item numbers to denote the maximum salaries! that different members of the staff may be paid enables him to discharge incompetent persons and engage others without the necessity of having an Order in Council in eaott instance, and that this method' has received: the endorsation of the Auditor General.
Instead of saying:	I want one clerk to
copy letters, another to stamp envelopes, and so on, he says: I want so many men at from $1,000 to $2,000 a year each. This means that we are substituting a commissioner for the Governor in 'Council. The chairman of the board, who is not under the control of the Civil Service Commission, may say,	as' is sametimes done in the Estimates, that notwithstanding	anything in
the Civil Service Act or any other law, $600,000 shall be paid out under the patronage system to the staff of the commission. I insist that this Act should cover every commission, and that no exception should be made unless set out in the statute creating the commission. Let us have a real Civil Service Act, not a mere camouflage which will make the people believe that something has been done and for which those who have promoted the Bill may take credit.
