The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Paragraphs (f) and (g) of section 2 read:
(f)	"Outside Service" means and includes the other officers, clerks and employees included in the public service, not being part of the Inside Service.
(g)	"Public Service" means and includes all officers, clerks or employees in the service of the Crown or of Parliament.
By reading that, we really have very little knowledge of -what may be included in the Outside Service. On the canals and in many other places in Canada we have men employed', some for eight months, others, for shorter term's. Some of them are called permanent employees and others temporary.
I should like to know under what heading they will come. Will they come under this Act?
Yes.

I do not want to be understood as opposing this measure. I have said that I agree with the principle of it, but I think we have, perhaps, gone a little far afield. The clamour throughout the country in the past has been, not so much in regard to the appointing of men to swing a bridge o.r run a post office, as against the patronage slate for all purchases in the various departments at Ottawa, as well as throughout Canada. In the past we have had to comply with that patronage *slate, and I quite agree with the Government in their endeavour to abolish it. We have, however, very little information in regard to this Bill, and the acting minister has acknowledged that it is, to a large extent, a temporary Bill. If we read the clauses respecting the Outside Service, we see that the commission, immediately after the passage of this legislation, is to get together and formulate rules and regulations in connection with the Outside Service. I entirely agree with the sentiments expressed this morning by the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Turriff), that such an important Bill as this, involving as much as if does, should not be brought up in the dying days of Parliament in the endeavour to have it rushed through. The members of this House are entitled to all possible .information before the Bill is permitted to become law, and I would seriously recom-

mend to the acting minister to take into consideration the .advice given this -morning toy the toon, member for Aseinilboia, to withdraw this measure for the present and refer the matter to- a committee of this House who may confer with the Civil Service Commission -and with the heads of the different departments and have the regulations and rules' all consolidated and brought down at the next session, as will evidently have to toe done. We can then deal intelligently with the situation. -Since the Order in Council -was passed a few months ago we [DOT]have been making appointments to the Outside Service in all parts of Canada. Why not let us go- on during the re-cess under this Order in Council as we have been doing? -Then perhaps toy the next session of Parliament we shall -have a better knowledge of how this -legislation will work out, especially if the committee sees fit to appoint a committee of this House to consult with the Civil Service and the heads of the different departments.

I am absolutely opposed to the withdrawal of this Bill. It is the duty of the present session of Parliament to p-ass- this- Civil Service Bill, because -of the solemn agreement entered into with the people of Canada. I do not see that -there is anything to be gained by standing this Bill over until the next session. As was suggested toy the Acting Minister of Finance, there may be some defects in the Bill, but I have never yet seen any Bill, except perhaps Bills relating to private legislation, in which there have not been some defects, -and which have not, from time to time, required amendment. The suggestion, of the hon. member -is that this Bill be reintroduced in-to this House -at the next session, and that a committee of members he appointed to work out a measure in the interests. of the country. If there are defects in this- Bill, I know of no method toy which those defects can he made more -apparent to the Government -and the public -than -by enacting the Bill and putting it into force. I know of no body of men more competent to observe the defects in the -operation of the Act than- the members of the Government -themselves, and more particularly the members of the Civil Service [Commission, who will have charge of the administration of the Act. If we find that the time between now and the prorogation or adjournment of Parliament is not sufficient for us to discuss and pass- this Bill, -then it is our duty to come back here in August, as was suggested by the Prime 
.Minister, in order to give the Bill full consideration. But it is the duty of this Government to the country and to the Civil (Service at laT-ge that this Bill be placed upon the statute hooks this- year and put into operation -as speedily as possible.

Like the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie), I desire- to see this Bill passed, because I am anxious to get back t-o Regina, and should not like to return to that city if this Bill is not passed, because I know -the attitude of my constituents in regard to this -matter. After the explanation of the Acting Minister of Finance as regards section 2, I find it quite easy for me to support it. As I understand his explanation, this Bill brings- within- its operation all the employees of the Dominion of Canada, with the exception of the deputy ministers, the Civil Service Commissioners, the Militia of Canada, and the railway employees, .and, as the hon. -member for Victoria (Sir -Sam Hughes) has said, the senators of the Dominion. The deputy ministers should be left out of the operation of this law, because, as a firm believer in what is termed the pyramid system of organization, I feel that this Parliament should hold right under its control a certain body -that will be directly responsible to it. As I take it, these deputy .ministers will, hereafter be responsible to the ministers, the ministers being undoubtedly responsible to this Parliament, so that we shall have direct control o-ver those deputy -ministers. If at any time a deputy does .something that he should not do, as we were told yesterday, by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ni-ckle) .that -one of them did, it would not take this Parliament very long to get rid of such a deputy minister, and in that way we would have the necesary efficiency in that particular department. The militia, of course, should he -exempted -from the operation of this legislation. The Civil Service Commisioners should also be exempted, because the commission should toe directly responsible -to this Parliament. I may be wrong, but I do not think w.e should ever attempt to bring the employees of the Government railways under the operations of this Act. Those railway employees should in my opinion, be under a separate commission, just as independent as this one will be, and just as -subject to Parliament, but absolutely free from political control or interference. Where we have such a large body of -men technically trained as railway men -are, we should not attempt to bring

them under the control of a commission such as this, which coul<i not attend to the work as efficiently as a commission of technically trained men, specially delegated for the purpose, could do. I think, therefore, everybody that should be reached by this legislation, is being reached. We should bring all of the Inside and Outside Services under the operation of such a Bill as this. The Bill may not be perfect, but I do not think that any law .that could be regarded as absolutely perfect was ever passed by this or any other Parliament.
If they were all perfect, there would he no need for us to come here year after year to improve them. We must therefore treat this Bill as we would any other Bill. It must be considered in relation to present conditions and we can make any amendments in the future that are deemed desirable. I have no doubt we shall find defects in the Act, but we can deal with them next year just as we are dealing with the Bill to-day. The people in the section from which I come are very anxious to have this Bill passed, because they have seen some of the evils of patronage. I do not know whether this Bill touches the question of patronage in the matter of buying supplies, hut that is a different matter altogether. Let us clean up patronage in the matter of appointments, and we can deal with the other matter later. I unhesitatingly support this Bill.

I suppose the public hangman comes under this clause. I think it is very important that we should include some one empowered to act as Civil Service executioner, for we know that many departments are over-manned.' In the Printing Department, for instance, I arh informed there are two hundred surplus men floating about doing nothing, and when I brought that fact to the notice of a responsible member of this Government he told me it would be political suicide to clean that department up. In the Statistics Branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce there are a hundred and thirty men doing what it takes only seventy-four men to do in the United States, and there would be between seven and eight hundred men in this branch in the United States if they engaged men on the scale we do in proportion to the amount of work to be done. I do not see in the Bill any provision for remedying these conditions. The hon. member for Lambton has said that the Bill will reduce our expenditure on the 'Civil Service by thirty or forty per cent. I have no doubt it should 113
be reduced to that extent, but I do not see any means provided in the Bill for doing so. Section 10 of Part 2 provides that the present status of employees shall be preserved. Section 25 deals with the employment of extra assistance. It may be necessary to have extra help in certain departments at certain times on account of the growing business of the country, but I think the main business of the commission should be first to deal with the overmanning of departments. I think they could set a fine example to all municipal governments in this country, because I think I am safe in saying that there is hardly a municipality where three men are not employed to do the work of two. I think this matter should be considered, while we are dealing with the definitions under this clause.

I listened attentively this morning to the criticisms of this Bill. Most of the critics were in favour of the principle of the Bill, they said. I do not wish to question their sincerity, but it seems to -me they took a very strange way of showing their love for the Bill. As the discussion proceeds, it seems plain either that we shall be here all summer or that the Bill will be talked out. I think in these strenuous times, when the news from the front is so serious, members of this House could be better. engaged than in wrangling over this or any other Bill. I am an enthusiastic supporter of the principle of this Bill and of the abolition of the patronage system. It would seem from the discussion that some have a lingering love for the old system. We have heard about the benefits of having appointments made on the recommendation of the member for the constituency. That sounds very well, but as a matter of fact it has not been the practise in the past. In the constituency I represent the recommendations have not been made by the member for the last thirteen or fourteen years. When I was rejected by the people of that constituency, it was- I who recommended the appointees, and not the member, and when I was elected as their representative I had nothing whatever to >s-ay about patronage; and that was the situation in nearly half the constituencies in Canada under the old system. I am very anxious,to see this Bill go through at once. Whatever defects there are in the Bill will appear when the Act is in operation, and we oan rectify them next session. This will not be the last session of this House, we hope. Let us put the Bill through at once and



get away, because I think we could be better employed elsewhere. But if the Bill is to be held up or talked out, and that seems to be the intention, I would beseech the Government to keep in force the Order in Council doing aw.ay with patronage. I am not much of a lover of Government by Order in Council, but the situation is such that I think the Government would be justified in retaining the Order in Council if this Bill does not pass this session. I am satisfied that the vast majority of the people of Canada would approve such action, and I am satisfied, notwithstanding all we have heard this morning, that a pronounced-majority of the members of this House are favourable to the principle of this Bill and favourable to the abolition of the system of patronage.

I absolutely agree with my hon. friend that we could be better engaged than m discussing this Bill. That is one of the main reasons I urged that the Bill be withdrawn, and I again ask the minister to withdraw it. So far as I can see we are operating just as effectively with respect to the Inside and Outside Service under the Order in Council passed two months ago, as we could operate under this Bill. The Government could apply the Order in Council, and then next session after we have discovered the defect in the system we could discuss the matter more intelligently. If it is not true that the Order in Council is as effective as this Bill, I withdraw my objection.

During the last election the.Prime Minister pledged himself to the elimination of patronage in appointments to the public service. This Bill has been introduced to implement that promise, and I therefore cannot acquiesce in the suggestion that it be withdrawn. It is true that we are now operating under the Order in Council, but that w-as largely a direction, and not an enactment, and there are grave doubts as to the porver of the Government to pass an Order in Council covering the appointments to the Civil , Service in the manner indicated in the Order in Council. It is therefore considered wise -and businesslike on the part of the Government to give statutory effect to the principle of the Order in Council. If this Bill were entirely new, I could appreciate the objections raised by hon. gentlemen. But ninety-five per cent of the clauses are old and have been the law for many years. The substance of the new clauses was set forth in the resolution upon which this Bill is founded, and we had quite a lengthy

discussion when that resolution was- moved. That was some four or five weeks ago. Therefore, I fail to appreciate the contention that the House is taken by surprise m being asked to enact this Bill. This morning there were some suggestions made as to clause 2, particularly the definition of "Civil Service." As stated this morning, paragraph (a) of section 2, which defines the term "Civil Service," is really not necessary, and so I propose that the clause be struck out. I therefore beg to move:
That paragraph (a) of section 1 be struck out; that paragraph (e) of section be amended by striking out the words "that part of the Civil Service" and inserting in place thereof the words "those officers, clerks or employees who are"; that paragraph (d) of section 2 be amended by striking out the word "Public" and substituting therefor the word "Civil" and by striking out the words "or Parliament" and also that the paragraphs he relettered from (a) to (f) inclusive.
I suggest the striking out of the words "or of Parliament," because that is covered by a subsequent clause.

The Acting Minister of Finance said that members have had considerable time to examine this Bill during the interval since the Bill was introduced, and also that there had been some discussion on the resolution. The -members of Parliament have been getting a little bit of information about this Bill, and about the activities of these gentlemen, and this is one of the things that I intend to bring before the House. This morning I made a reference to a letter that was written by a member of the Civil Service threatening, and endeavouring to intimidate, the members of this House into supporting this measure. We have also heard speeches in the House endeavouring to intimidate threatening that if it did not carry immediately this House would be prorogued until next August. Well, we are not afraid of having this House prorogued until next August. We have had sessions lasting almost a year, and that sort of thing does not go down with the members of this House at all. We might continue in session for four or five weeks longer with benefit to the public interest. There are. many things that we might go into and discuss; for	instance, the appointment of a curator of German property which has never been made although vi'e have been at war fo-r four years. A committee of this House, might spend a few weeks investigating some of the commissions that have been operating under this Government. In reference to the

question of patronage, there is patronage and patronage. The moist odious form of patronage is nepotism. The outcry of the public against tlhe administration of pat-ranage has not been in reference to- the appointment of people. I challenge any of those hon. members who have been talking about 'the evils .and troubles of patronage to point oat one single case that has occurred in 'the last eight or ten years where _ .any great mistake has been made in reference to appointments. There is such a thing as patronage in the Public Works Department and matters of that kind and those are the things that the people are talking -about. The Civil Service is divided into two parts, the In-si'de and the Outside Service. The Inside Service has been under the commission and the Outside Service has not. Anybody who knows anything about these services will unhesitatingly say that in the great -majority of cases the men of the Outside Service have higher qualifications -and do much harder work than those in the Inside 'Service, .although they do not get the same money at all. They . have had this organization formed amongst the civil .servants to get a little rise in pay. For my part, with reference to the Outside Service, I think we might have adopted the principle .adopted in England and given them a war bonus of, say, ten per cent, because everybody knows that it is very difficult for the members of the Outside Service to live -under 'the conditions that exist at the present time. Instead of giving them a ten per cent rise you give them this Bill, which means that when they ask for bread you give them 'a stone. There are two kinds of patronage. This Bill is the result of an agitation that has been carried on by the Civil Service organization. The circular I read this morning shows that -that organization i-s endeavouring to intimidate members of Parliament. I shall go further and read yo-u a letter that members of this organization have issued in order 'to carry o-n their agitation and to extend it to 'all parts of the country. I hold in my hand a letter issued by the secretary of the Canadian Postmasters' Association, in which he says:	.
Aurora, Ont., April 19, 1918.
Dear Postmaster:
Postmasters more than any other class feel the hardships of war prices owing to the small allowances given them by the Government.
It has beenv decided by our Association that the time has come when we should make a determined effort to secure relief.
113*
You must help if success is to be achieved that is, if you desire it, we believe most if not all do-you ask how-well by writing to the Member for your district at Ottawa. Explain the amount of work done in your office each day-show the cost of hired help, if any- duties of office, hours of service, rent paid, and the amount paid you each month-compare the Government. pay with what you could earn with the same labour on a farm or at some other occupation, but do not find fault with any Postmaster's salary as compared with your own. Write this letter in your own words but do it at once.
If you have a local paper published in your town or village will you kindly see the editor or publisher and have him print an article calling the attention of the public and the Government to the hardships imposed upon us through the adoption of commissions dating back to Confederation-explain to him how the war has added many millions of letters and circulars, etc., sent out by the different departments of the Government upon which there is so much extra work but not a cent of pay. [DOT]
Now for a big united effort and don't fear to talk plain to your Member. If you feel like quitting your job in disgust, say so. When you have done this sign the attached counterfoil and mail it to me.
This came from the town of Aurora, which I understand is also the native town of the Deputy Postmaster General. In every other department a similar agitation, a similar propaganda, is carried on, and we know very well that the agitation has blossomed forth in respect to this Bill. Now, hon. members will wonder what is going to happen to the patronage business? When this House divests itself of its power, as it is going to do under the Bill, it will have deprived itself of one of its ancient privileges and prerogatives-the right to say who shall be .appointed to positions in the public service. Then the- right of appointment will come not from the Crown, not from the minister, but from the Civil Service Commission. Will the commission make the appointment? I am going to tell hon. members that -when the commission want to appoint somebody in their districts they will send a letter to the postmaster or the custom house official there, and these men will nominate appointees to the Civil Service in Ottawa. That is how the appointments are going to be made. Is not that patronage? One of the most prominent men in the city of Toronto was filling the columns of the papers a few months ago with weird appeals .and complaints about the appointment of people to the Civil Service, and at the very same time he was seeking the appointment of his own daughter to a job in the Civil Service, and she got the position. There is a lot of hypocrisy in this world, but I think I am talking

to a lot of hard-headed men who do not take any stock in hypocrisy. Will the public interest be better served by having appointments made by the member, through the minister who is responsible, or by leaving the appointing in the hands of irresponsible people who will select whoever they like?
Now, a word about appointments to these commissions, and which are not to come under the operation of the Civil Service Act, although those staffs will. I think it is time we called a halt to the appointment of commissions for everything. This attempt at the devolution of responsibility from the Government to commissions, is something the country is wide awake to now and is taking notice of. The other day as I sat at luncheon in one of the prominent clubs -in this city, a gentleman who occupied the seat alongside of me, .said: " Currie, you notice all these people who are sitting here; let us count how many representatives of commissions are sitting around this room?" We started to count, and we named nineteen of them. Each one of these commissions performs functions that should be discharged by some department of this Government over which the Government should have authority to rule and as to whose proceedings they should have a say. This Parliament is becoming nothing but a rubber stamp to initial the doings of these different bodies.	[DOT]
The gentlemen to whom the hon. gentleman has referred were all clu'b men.

They were all club men
sitting round a table in that club. You can go there every day and count nineteen or twenty-five of them if you wish. I think the time has come for Parliament to put itself on record, to speak plainly and act openly. This Civil Service Commission is another commission whose hands we are strengthening .and to whom we .are furnishing greater powers. What is happening alreadyf Everybody knows well, and nobody better ihan the ministers of the Crown, that there are several services so organized here that the members of the service, from the deputy down, will defy a minister and evade what he asks them to do, and' he has no recourse. There are many men going around the Oivil Service who do not do a day's work, in fact they are doing nothing 'but stirring up trouble, and at the same time drawing money from the people of the country. The people would be very much shocked to know that
I.Mr. Currie.]
but it is a fact. These men do not do a minute's work, let alone a day's work, in their departments.	They are walking
around here, going to public meetings and organizing various societies, and setting themselves up as censors of the public, and all that sort of thing. If the minister in charge	of	a department .says a word as to- what is happening he is met immediately with a threat that the majority of his staff will walk out. Talk about the tyranny of the labour unions. There is one thing about the labour unions, they have men over them who are sensible and will not let them walk out without cause-they are subject to discipline. But this Bill takes the control of the discipline -of the Civil Service entirely out of the hands of a minister; it will deprive him of all power to do anything with the men under him. As I said you -are loading a gun that has not got a trigger ,on it. You cannot fire these men even if you want to, they will stay in the service for all time.
The Acting Minister of Finance has said that this Bill has sheen a long time before the House. Certainly it has, and the longer it is before the House the more we realize what a great mistake was made in introducing it. The Prime Minister is a very human man with a big heart. Very often his attention is called to something, and great pressure is brought to bear upon him to- carry into effect what is sought. The propaganda to which I referred is worked upon, him, in the same way as it is worked upon the members. He receives thousands of letters about a certain thing, and in the fullness of his heart he decides that it is .better to do what is asked than to have difficulty. The demands of the Civil Service have been before this House for many years. A few years ago experts were brought in from the four quarters of the earth to go through the Civil Service and to ipake recommendations with the object of rendering it more efficient. The experts went to the departments and they made recommendations'. Those recommendations were laid on, the table of the House and Parliament was- supposed joyfully to .adopt them. ,1 do not thinlk any one of the recommendations made at that time has ever been carried out. There may be one, hut -if s-o, I do not know of it. Why the Civil Service organizations were so strong the ministers could not take action. As I have already said, the ministers -are defied and they know that as well as I do. What we should do with the present Bill is to put

power in the hands of the ministers so that they shall have the power of dismissal.
We have the power.

But you do not exercise
it. I can name two or three men who have made themselves offensive to the whole Canadian public,. and you do not dare to dismiss them.
Name.

I could name them, but I will not do so. It would only make trouble and I am too good a Canadian to start trouble unnecessarily. But these men have done things that they should not have done, and the organ of the Civil Service in Ottawa is continually filled with denunciations of the Government. I would like to take that journal and read its contents to the members of the House, and I have no doubt at tall they would throw this Bill out in five minutes. The columns of that journal are continually filled with attacks not only on members of the Government, but on gentlemen on the other side. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in office they often received a broadside from, behind consisting of high explosives from the journal of the Civil Service. Those hon. gentlemen when they were in power could not do anything in their departments but what we of the Opposition knew all about it, showing that ir any members of the Civil Service are not true to their salt. I do not class all the members of the Civil Service in that category. Many of them are entitled to the highest praise, big men, who are receiving far too little money for the services they are performing. These men are doing -three-fourths of the work, and the other cne-fourth is disttibuted amongst chaps who do not do anything but walk around and wok nice. Some of the members of the House are sympathetic towards this Bill, and other similar measures, because, they are of the opinion they are going to , pass something which will be of benefit to the public. It is not the appointment of men to office that has raised the cry about patronage. That cry has originated from such jobs as the building of sawdust wharves, and the expenditures of large sums of money on works that are not necessary in the interests of the public at all. That is what constitutes patronage, so called, and not the appointment of a few civil servants to office. In my opinion the people of this country will not stand for the appointment of men to the public service not being in the hands of the member whom they have chosen and whom they have
made responsible. They certainly will not approve of handling those appointments over to the local postmaster or the local custom house officer instead of to the member for the constituency.
That is the system that is shown clearly through the method1 of organization they have introduced, and if the hon. member for Strath Perth had the means of finding out how the appointment he mentioned was made, no doubt he would find that some postmaster wrote a private letter to the department.
It was one of the deputies who undertook to do the job.
Did the deputy know the man?

No, he did not, or he would not have appointed him.
Mr. 'CURRIE: How did he get his name at all? Who sent the man's name to- him?
You will have to ask the deputy.
It was probably the postmaster.

No- -chance.
Mr. -CURRIE: However, that is- the condition of affairs, -and if members of this House feel like absolving themselves of all responsibility for -appointments, and- turning them over to postmasters, customs' and excise officers, landing waiters and -men like that, of course, they may go- ahead and do it. That -is what this Bill provides. If the acting minister 'thinks there should still be one particle of responsibility -attaching to members of this House-and some responsibility -should attach to them in their own ridings-'then let the Bill stand. We have an Order in 'Council dealing with 'this- question now. I say, let us try out the system outlined in that Order in Council and -see how it works out for six or seven -months, and then we will know whether -or not it is a good system. The Government can cancel an Order in Council a't any time, but if you pa-s-s a Bill like this it is necessary to oo-me back to- Parliament to have the -matter righted. That is my argument, and I think I have put on the records of the House sufficient evidence ito show hon. gentlemen how the oracle will be worked in their ridings. I do not think -any m-an of -sense would stand up in this Bouse and sup-port that method o-f patronage as the proper one as -ag-amst the method that has prevailed.

I have listened to what the Acting Minister of Finance said a moment ago, and he needs not to he assured of my full sympathy for Civil Service reform. But I do not think he is backed up by his own friends. There seems to be a cleavage between the goody-goody element in the Unionist party and the other fellows. Indeed, it seems very clear that the Prime Minister himself, who, my hon. friends claim, is in favour of the Bill, is not much enamoured of this legislation, otherwise he would be in his seat and would stand by my hon. friend and see that the Bill is carried through. What have we seen since the beginning of this debate? I have seen my friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid), smiling quietly not saying a word. Of course, the railway employees do not come under the jurisdiction of the commission; they will remain under the close jurisdiction of the Minister of Railways and Canals. When my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan) said we must not expect the railway men to be put under the Civil Service Commission because they are experts and technical employees, and so on, that the commission could not deal with them, he does not seem to know that the technical officers of every department come under the jurisdiction of this same commission. I say to the acting minister: If you want to .abolish patronage, do. not give us a sham, give us the real article, and put every railway employee from one end of Canada to the other under this commission, otherwise you will not be sincere in the eyes of the people. The acting minister, turning to his friends-I do not know if he was addressing himself to the Tories or to the Grits-addressing my friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) with some severity, said that the Prime Minister had given a solemn pledge at the last general election that there would be Civil Service reform. Surely my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance is not serious. He knows just as well as I do that the pledges given by the right hon. gentleman who lead's the Government cannot be taken seriously by the country more especially on this question of Civil Service reform. He should remember when we were sitting together on this side of the House,, and poking the ribs of his present leader. He recollects that in 1907 the Prime Minister, in his' celebrated Halifax platform, ,a platform which was engineered to defeat my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) just as much as his friends on this side of the House, had for the goody-goody element of

the country a Civil Service reform plank. Hero is what he said, when my hon. friend was the running mate of the right hon. gentleman in Halifax, that is in 1911, when he was running against him.
Oh, oh.

The Prime Minister
said-

I rise to a point of
order. What paper is the hon. gentleman reading from?
I am just using a refresher.

Mr. Chairman, I think I am entitled to the name of the document from which the hon. gentleman is reading, or else he should lay it on the Table.
Mr. 'LEMIEUX:	iMy hon. friend is too
fresh.
I may be too fresh, but I would not he ashamed, to give the name of any document I quoted from.

speechtext: * Order. The hon. member for Maisonneuve has the floor, and no interruption, of course, can be allowed without the permission of the member who has the floor. Hon. gentlemen will remember that the same rule which applies in the House applies also in committee. While I .am on my feet I shall ask the hon. member for Maisonneuve not to wander too far away from the clause under consideration.
I am simply reading the article for the benefit of the acting minister.

Yon need not
read that article for me; it was read the other day and I remember it quite well.
Are you in favour of the Bill?

I am in. favour of the
Bill, but not of a sham reform. Will the hon. gentleman put railway employees under the proposed Act?
I gave good reasons why they should not come under it.

If this Bill passes it assumes to place under the Civil Service Commission some 70,000 public servants throughout the Dominion. The commission employs him here.

The commission is

Mr. PEiDLOW: I take it that the management of the business of the Dominion Government is no different in principle from that of any other large business concern in the country. You must have centralized authority having sole control and being supreme in arranging matters of organization, filling vacant offices, making promotions, carrying out dismissals and dispensing with supernumeraries. I think it is the intention of the Acting Minister of Finance to make provision by means of this Bill along those lines. The Oivil Service Commission is the best power to take the place of centralized authority, and corresponds to an individual in a personal organization. When you begin to develop the business -along definite lines you must -appoint heads of departments. Now, the business- of this country has been developing for years, and at the present time is developing along larger lines than- it has ever done before. Consequently you must organize new departments under special heads. If you want to hold the -special heads-deputies, or whatever you like to call them-responsible for the working out of their departments you -must place them in control of those departments. We had an exhibition in one of the departments of the Government a few days ago of the mistake of following a different course. In the Department of Labour a junior employee upset the whole machinery of the department and caused the dismissal of the best department head that the Government has had for many years past, a man who gave good service to the Government. I do not wish to oppose the dropping of this section, but I wish to say a word over its funeral. During the last session I listened to the great representative of the French Government preaching democracy-Mr. Viviani. I shortly after listened to the eloquent representative of Great Britain. They told us that this was a war for democracy. Democracy means representative and responsible government. Yet, this is an attempt largely to set up a bureaucracy. hung back and opposed any change and have carried on in the same old way. The ministers should be supreme t>ver the deputies. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: I desire to make a suggestion which, in the light of actual experience, I think will improve the section referred to. The first Civil 'Service Act, as the minister knows, was passed in 1908 under the Government of which I happened to be a member, and the administration of the Act was .attached to the department of which, at that time, I had charge. It was found that there were a good many anomalies in the departments owing to the fact that the same system of organization and classification was not carried out throughout the service. I take it that this new section is designed to. remove those anomalies, and secure a levelling up throughout the service. That will be difficult unless some specific direction is given to the commission, so as to secure similar organization and classification in each department-in other words, so that the anomaly may not be presented, for instance, of men in different departments hut doing the same class of work being paid different salaries. There are many such anomalies in the service in Ottawa, and I would suggest adding after the words "public service" in line twelve, the words: " Such organization, as far as possible, to follow the same general principles in all departments." If some authority such as that be not inserted, the commission will find it very difficult, indeed, to secure cooperation in all the departments.

I am willing to accept the hon. gentleman's suggestion, and I move that there he added after the words "public service" on the twelfth line, the words:
Such organization as far as possible to follow the same general principles in all1 branches of the Civil Service.
Amendment agreed to.

A question was raised as to the reorganization being made. Reorganization is effected by consultation on the part of the heads of the departments,
or the deputy heads, with the commission. Then subsection 2 provides:
(No change shall he made in the organization of any department until it has been so reported upon by the said Commission.
That reorganization is in force and effect the moment it is approved by the Governor in Council. Following the reorganization, there will have to he a classification of the various employees who have heretofore been in the department, as provided in subsection 3. After this is done and the organization is complete, why not submit that organization and classification, with all the recommendations of both the commission and the deputy heads, to the Governor in Council?
That would be simpl-y going over tihe work a second time. Nothing would be accomplished by that.

The fact that a plan of a house has been drawn does not exempt from accepting delivery of the house .to complete the contract. Section as amended agreed to.

There is no change in this section. It is the same as in the present Civil Service Act.

The pleasure of any party that is in power.

On section 12-Addition to salary on appointment :

Is there any change here from the old Act?
Mr. A. K. 'MACLEAN: The section is just the same, except that the sum .stated in the third line is $200 instead of $500.

On section 14-Appointments to be on probation:
Mr. A. K .MACLEAN: I move to strike out the words in subsection 1: " And the cause of the rejection shall be reported by the depulty head to the commission," and to add at the end of that subsection the words: " and the cause of rejection, or the reason for extending the period of probation shaill be reported by the deputy head to the commission." The clause does not state whether or not the commission shall investigate the cause of rejection as reported by the deputy head. The deputy head may be ill-tempered-people grow old and do not retain the same equanimity as when they are young. The Commission shall decide whether the name of a rejected person shall he struck off 
the list as unfit for the service generally or whether he shall he allowed a trial in some other .position for which he may he eligible.

On second thought, this subsection is not so clear as it seemed to me at first. iMr. A. K. MACLEAN: However, if the committee think that there should be an amendment, the words " after investigation " might go in after the word " shall ", in tlhe first line of subsection 3, which would then read:
(3) The Commission shall after investigation, decide whether the name of the rejected person-

On section 16-Professional and technical positions:
I move that the word "competitive" be inserted after the word "without" in the 13th line of this section, so that it will read "either with or without competitive examination."
Is this not against the principle laid down in this Bill? The deputy head is supposed to accept the man selected by the commission.
The only difference between this clause and the clause in the old Act is that the approval is to be by the commission instead of by the Governor in Council.

Why -does the minister put in the word "competitive"? Would a surveyor' who is a Bachelor of Science be expected to enter a competitive examination in order to take a position in the Department of Public Works?

I would put the same question with regard to architects and translators. When the old Act had been in force only a few months we were in need of a competent translator for the Labour Gazette. I suggested the appointment of the late Mr. Lanctot, and the question arose whether a translator was a technical officer. I submitted that a competent translator was a technical officer; the matter was discussed in Council and referred to the Minister of Justice, Sir Allen Ayles-worth, who prepared a memorandum on the subject which may now be found in the Department of Justice. Would an architect have to pa?s a competitive examination before he could be appointed to a position in the Public. Works Department? It is represented to me that under this Bill he would.
This clause provides that the commission has authority to make such appointments without competitive examination.

When departments require officers with professional or technical knowledge, in some cases advertisements are placed in the press and applicants are requested to communicate with 9 p.m. the Civil Service Commission.
If two or three of the applicants appear to have equal merits, the commission would likely adapt the procedure which I outlined last night, that of appointing a board to consider the relative merits of each. In that case some sort of examination
might be prescribed. The commission are not obliged to do that, however.	.
Wherein does this section differ from the old section 21?
"The Commission" is inserted in place of "The Governor in Council." That is practically the only change.

I think that is a mistake. The old section was intended to check the appointment of experts by requiring the submission of each case to the Governor in Council. The members of Council, sitting around a table, will not agree to the appointment of a man as an expert if he really is not an expert. I had occasion last year to look into the administration of section 21 under the present Act, and I found that considerable abuse existed.
In a return brought down to the House it was shown that 175 appointments of so-called experts had been made under section 21. I found that the appointees were [DOT]mostly men who were over age and who were receiving small salaries such as- $1,100, $1,200 or $1,500 per annum. They were not experts at all, but they were favourites of the administration and they were called "experts" to* avoid examination and placed in those positions under section- 21. If you open the door any wider -and allow the commission- to appoint, without examination, any person that they may call an expert, we might -as well dispense with the Civil Service Act altogether. I would suggest to the minister that he maintain the language of section 21, so that there will be -some check in the appointment of these technical officers.

I would submit to my hon. friend that the old section, to which he refers was claimed- by many members of Parliament to be subject to -abuse. It .was urged that frequently men were promoted upon the ground that they were -technical or professional officers and, on the recommendation of the deputy head and the approval of the Governor in Council, such men might be promoted t-o a higher position- and receive -a higher salary. The purpose of this new section was to remove that power from the Governor in Council, which is always a political body. I thought the House would agree that the approval 6-hall be placed in the hands of the commission! just to avoid possible abuse. I think this section is- much preferable to the old section 21.	.

'Mr. MURPHY: There is just this albout it, that the remodelled section may lead in its operation to a conflict between the Civil Service Commission .and the deputy head, because it makes the appointment rest on the recommendation of the deputy minister. I am aware that the suggestion has been made to my hon. friend, possibly he has not had time to consider it, and I do not want to press, it, but I think it proper to bring it before the comlmittee, so -that when it is sought to- invoke this section, the intervention of the- deputy minister should be confined to asking for an appointment.
M.r. A. K. MACLEAN: I propose changing the word " recommendation " to " request."

I appreciate what my
ihon. friend says as being a move in the direction of meeting the .situation which I am about to disclose, that is, that the deputy minister should be restricted to asking for an .appointment in a certain grade andi not for the appointment of a certain individual. That feature of the appointment should be determined by the commission, and not by the deputy minister. The .section, as it stands, would prevent that being done by the commission. I beg to move:
That the word ''recommendation" in the tenth line be struck out and the word "request" be inserted!

If, in these technical examinations such as the one illustrated, a first-class man was an applicant, I doubt very much if he would 'Submit to enter into a competitive examination, especially if .he had university or other qualifications which proved his status beyond peradven-ture. I know I would not if I were making application. I would say that I had got beyond that stage in my professional career. I do not think it is desirable to put in the word " competitive."

I would like to see the
words " professional' dr technical " in the ninth line defined. W.e are simply trying to avoid a difficulty by not defining those words. I wonder, .if the question were

asked the members of this committee individually, if there would be two opinions alike. . If we do not assume the responsibility of defining those words, how will the commission define them? I would suggest amending the first clause by adding to it a paragraph <iefining those words, " professional or technical," or else putting at the end of section 16 a definition of those words. It is no use trying to avoid the difficulty, it will come before the commission.

Will my hon.
friend offer the committee a definition of the words " professional or technical?" I do not think it is possible to draft a section which would meet his suggestion. It rests with the commission to decide whether the knowledge and ability requisite for any position is professional or technical. I do not see how you could possibly define the words.

The difficulty arose in regard to section 21 in connection with the famous case in the Militia Department. An issue was raised -between the minister and the commission as to the definition in connection with the appointment of a military tailor. I do not think they got beyond the regulations.

Those words were used in the British Civil Service Act and in the United States Civil Service Act, and I do not think either the British Parliament or the United States Congress has been .able to find any words to define the idea.

What necessity is there for technical officers in the Outside Service. I had the honour of sitting in this House at the time the original Act was passed, and it was represented to this House that occasionally eminent engineers or men from the outside would be required to do such important work as designing the Quebec bridge or other work of that kind; that such men would not submit themselves to an examination before any commission, and that section 21 was necessary, when a case of that kind arose, to enable the Government to secure the services of an eminent technical expert for carrying on such work. It -strikes me that we do not require the section so far as the Outside Service is concerned.
Take the engineers of the Public Works Department.
They are in the Inside Service.

No, not in the several provinces. There are engineers in the Marine and Fisheries Department. In the Outside Service many technical officers are required, and, of course, a great many in the Inside Service.

Take the case of the
Marine and Fisheries Department. Inspectors of boilers and hulls have now to pass a special examination provided by the department. Will they now be examined by the commission?

I do not see that the
section is improved by the amendment that has been moved. The Minister of the Interior may make a request for a surveyor and it is for the commission to do the rest. Under the old Act, the appointment was made by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the minister of the department.
The recommendation of the minister was based on the report in writing of the deputy head, and the man, before being 'appointed, had to get a certificate from the Civil Service Commission that he was qualified to fill the position. When all these steps had been taken we had a record showing what the deputy head had reported in writing to the minister, the minister's recommendation, the certificate o.f qualification by the commission, and the Order in Council making the appointment. To-day all a minister has to do is to make a request to' the commission that he requires an expert accountant, we will say, and we have no record showing what the man is required for or whether he is qualified. I think the clause ought to be further amended so that if a request is to be made it shall be made in writing, stating the reasons and the particular service for which the man is required.

I think this clause is preferable to section 21 in the old Act, which permitted .a man to be appointed when the qualifications required were " professional, technical, or otherwise peculiar." We are striking out the words " or otherwise peculiar."
That is not what I object to. I say the request should be in writing.

Under the old Act it was possible for the deputy head to read almost anything into the wording of section 21, thereby rendering the section liable to great abuses. We are here restricting the
appointments to those offices requiring professional or technical qualifications.

That is all right. What I object to is that an appointment can be made at the request of the deputy head. Under the old Act the recommendation was made by the minister upon the report of bis deputy, and then the applicant had to get a certificate of qualification from the commission. The section reads:
If the deputy head reports that the know* ledge and1 ability requisite for the position are wholly or in part professional, technical or otherwise peculiar, the Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the head of the department 'based on the report in writing of the deputy head, may appoint a person to the position without competitive examination and without reference to the age limit, provided the said person obtains from the Commission a certificate, to be given with or without examination, as is determined toy the regulations of the Commission, that he possesses the re-i quisite knowledge and ability and is duly qualified as to health, character and habits.
The deputy head had to make a report in writing to the minister showing the necessity for appointing a man with technical or professional knowledge. The record was there in writing. But under this section all the deputy head has to do is to send in a request for a technical man and the commission, may appoint him. I do>
not object to substituting the commission for the Governor in Council, but I want to know for what particular purpose the expert accountant or land surveyor is required and what branch of the service he is going to be employed in.

Under the old
Act it was necessary for the report to be in writing, because the 'Governor in Council had to approve the appointment. If we compelled the deputy head to make a report in writing to the commission to the effect that a technical officer was required for some particular work it would rather tie the hand's of the commission. A member of the 'Civil Service 'Commission informs me that just a few days ago they were requested to appoint a technical officer, but upon investigation they Ifoundj that the work was not of a professional or technical nature. I think it is 'better not to embarrass the commission by a report from the deputy head as to the necessity for a technical man. The commissioners should be allowed to decide whether or not it is a technical position.

Perhaps I did not make myself clear. The minister says that a report in writing had to he made because



the recommendation had to go before Council. We all know that, the report in writing was to enlighten the minister, so that he could discuss the matter before the Governor in Council when he made his recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the old section say that the commission shall certify that the man required is a professional or technical man? I would not object to the section in the old Act if we gave the commission power to decide whether or not the man required was a professional or technical man.

speechtext: But under the old Act the commission had no say as to whether the office is really one requiring a technical or professional man. The insertion of this word "request" means that the deputy is going to ask for
f(Mr. Bureau.]
a certain man. Then the commission, will send a man and say: "We certify that Mr. John Jones is a chartered accountant having all the qualifications necessary to fulfil the requisition sent in toy the Deputy Minister of Finance."

The argument of the hon. memlber for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) presupposes that the Civil Service Commission are going to make wholesale appointments to the Civil Service for which there is no justification.
Not at all.

I do not want it to
go on record that I am advocating leaving the matter in the hands of the Governor in Council or that I am afraid that the Civil Service Commission are going to make wholesale appointments. On the contrary, I want to help them' and I want to trust them. They will make an appointment at the request of the deputy minister. The deputy minister makes a request and I *want that request to be made in writing, stating exactly what the position is that he wants to fill. I beg to move:
That clause 16 be amended by adding, after, the word "request" the words "in writing", and after words "deputy head" the words! "giving his reasons for such request."

This section will now, I understand, apply to the Outside Service as well as the Inside Service. 11 p.,m. his powers and duties under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. The Auditor General cannot be dismissed except by a vote of Parliament.
The Auditor General is really not a deputy head.
He is given the position of deputy head for the purposes of this Act. All persons who are in charge of a number of employees are called deputy heads.
I direct the attention of the Government to this so that the argument may not afterwards be made that the dismissal of the Auditor General was provided for or intended by this section.

Section agreed to.
On section 31-suspensions:

I move:
That, In clause (a) of subsection 1, the following words he stricken out: "or from the receipt of his salary."
They do not seem to serve any good purpose there. The words rather suggest that a man might be performing his duty

by working in a department and not receiving hie salary. That would hardly be fair.
Amendment agreed to.

I beg to move:
That in the first line of subsection 2 after the word "suspension" the words "with the reasons therefor" be inserted, and that after? the word "reported," the words "in writing'' be inserted.
The subsection will then read:
All oases of suspension with the reasons therefor shall be reported in writing by the deputy head to the Commission.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 32-commission to control staff:

This is an entirely new clause. In this Bill we have so far been dealing with the Civil Service Commission and the commissioner or commissioners. This section says: " or other members composing any commission or board appointed by the Governor in Council." What commission or what board will that be?

This would apply to any commission appointed by the Governor in Council. It is designed to put the commissioner or commissioners in the position of deputy heads under this Act. For instance, one or more of the pension commissioners would make all such recommendations as are made under this Act by deputy ministers.

That does not answer my question. Power is here given to the Civil Service Commission to "oversee and direct the officers, clerks and employees under its, his or their control." By this section this power is also given to " other members composing any commission or board." Why does the minister not say:
" or the commissioner or head of the commission appointed by the Governor in Council?"
I understand that there will be a commissioner who will have all the power of the deputy head, so that he will replace him in the department.
In a department, the deputy head has to- make that request. In the oominiesion or board, any member of the oommiesion or board may make it?

Yes.
(Mr. BUREAU: I should think that the chairman of the Railway Board, or in hie absence, the vice-chairman, would make the request. I d-o not think it would! be well if any member of the commission might make requests. By this section we are giving members composing any commission or board appointed by the Governor in Council wider powers than the deputy heads now have. The duties of the deputy heads are defined by Act of Parliament, but here you have members of a commission or board each acting as an independent deputy head.
What does my hon. friend suggest?

I would suggest that the section read:
The -Civil Service Commission, the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission or the acting Chairman, and the Chairman of any board or commission appointed by the Governor in Council, or the acting chairman for the time? being.
Mr. DAVI-S: If in line 28, after the word "conferred," the following words:	"and
be subject to all the duties imposed " be added, so that the clause would read:
And shall with respect to such officers, clerks and employees have all1 the .powers conferred and be subject to all the duties imposed' by this Act on the deputy head of a departr meat.
Would that not meet the case?

That does not affect my suggestion. My idea is to have the head of

a commission or board or some one acting in his stead, perform the duties and take the responsibility.
In some cases there is only one commissioner.
Then so much the easier.

I think this section is entirely superfluous. We have now the Civil Service Commission with a head properly appointed, and certainly he has all the powers necessary for the working of that commission. Now you are making him and the two other members of that commission deputy ministers. In the case of a commission with half a dozen men they would all be deputy ministers. That seems to be creating confusion unnecessarily. I think the Order in Council appointing any commission should define its powers.

Having in mind clause 3 of section 4, I beg to move that after the word "conferred" in section 32, there be inserted the words "and be subject to all the duties imposed." Clause 3 of section 4 reads:
The deputy heads and alt other officers and employees in the Public Service shall give the Commission such access to their respective departments and offices and such facilities, assistance and information as the Commission may require for the performance of its duties.
Amendment stands.
Section stands.
On section 34-Oaths.

I object to schedule "B,'' which reads as follows:
And that I will not, without due authority in that behalf, disclose or make known any matter or thing- which comes to my knowledga by reason of my employment as (as the case may be).
We do not want a civil servant to be a spy, but at the same time jie is an officer paid by the Government of this country to fulfil his duties conscientiously. This oath of secrecy would prevent him from divulging any scandalous proceeding, we will say, that came under his nQtice in the performance of his duties.
This is applicable to the Clerk of the Privy Council.

It extends to other employees. Clause 2 reads:
In the case of the Clerk of -the Privy Council, and all officers, clerks and employees under him, and in the case of any officer, clerk or employee of whom the Governor in Council requires the same, there shall be added to the [DOT] oath at the asterisks, in the form of the oath
in the said Schedule A, the words contained in Schedule B. to this Act.

That is, when
designated by the Governor in Council for special reasons. This has always been the law, and I think it is a very good provision.
I should like a better reason than that from my hon. friend.

What force does my hon. friend attach to the words " without due authority in that behalf '>
in schedule B?

A civil servant may discover in the performance of his duties some gross disregard of the public weal; something scandalous may be going on, but he may be debarred by the deputy head or some other person in authority from divulging what he has seen. He might say " I am under oath of secrecy and cannot divulge these things." I quite agree that there must be secrecy in some things. For instance, the Clerk of the Privy Council cannot divulge what takes place in Council. If it should apply only to the Clerk of the Privy Council I would raise no objection, but this subsection is not at all clear. I am only raising the point in order to make it clearer. It applies to "any officer, clerk or employee of whom the Governor in Council requires the same."
The Dominion Police force, for instance.

I quite understand that detectives must take an oath of secrecy and must not divulge what takes place. You ought to make it clear so that there will be no ambiguity. The Government might appoint a commission or a hoard and the Governor in Council might direct the deputy head to- give special instructions to the men employed under him not to divulge what should take place.
They would have to go before the Clerk of the Privy Council and take an affidavit to that effect? A mere instruction would not he of any use.

My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) can understand how and why there might be many officials in the Naval Service or the Militia Department who should be bound to secrecy. This section has been in the statute for a long time; it has not created any difficulty in the past and I -think it is a very wise provision.
