speechtext:
Take the case of confidential documents being sent down to the King's Printer to be printed; it is necessary

to have all the clerks in that department bound over to secrecy.

I do not object so much to that, but I would like to know the reason why the law is being changed. In the old law it is provided that the officer shall take and subscribe to the oath of allegiance and also the oath contained in schedule C, which is as follows:
I... .solemnly and sincerely swear that I will faithfully and honestly fulfil the duties which
devolve upon me as	and that I will not
ask or receive any sum of money, services, recompense or matter or thing whatsoever,, directly or indirectly in return for what I have done or may do in the discharge of any of the duties of my said office, except my salary or what may he allowed me by law or by an order of the Governor in Council.
I think that is a wise oath. I would like to know the reason why that oath, as well as the oath of allegiance, has been suppressed.
The oath of allegiance is referred to in connection with section 34, but it is not in the schedule. We will insert the oath of allegiance when we reach it.	.
Surely the oath of allegiance is in the schedule.
The text is not given, but it is referred to in the section.

I cannbt understand why that schedule A is amended. With reference to schedule B, wherein the officer declares that he will not make known any matter or thing which comes to his knowledge by reason of his employment, why should a man be debarred from telling his superior, or the deputy minister, if anything occurs to the detriment of the service? He is precluded from doing that now. He has to close his eyes to anything that takes place.
That is exactly what I am saying.
The schedule will stand.
You will amend the form?
Yes.
Then how can we pass the clause? The clause is subject to certain conditions and those conditions are contained in the schedule.
You can put in any conditions you like.
But schedules A and B are part of the clause. If you pass the clause you cannot change them.
My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance says he is going to make new sections.

Section agreed to.
On section 35-Voting at elections permitted, but partisan work forbidden:

I think the last words in that section " dismissed from the public service," aTe sufficient. All that is necessary is to provide is that the person violating the provisions of this section shall be deemed guilty of an offence and shall be dismissed from the public service.

Does that mean that he is debarred from taking part in a municipal election?
'Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: I think not.
Should you not mention that?
No.
It says in any Dominion or provincial election.
But it does not say that he is not debarred from taking part in any municipal election.
It is better as it is; he is at liberty to do so.
He is not debarred.

The clause, I believe, has been in the law for some time, but I happen to know that in a matter of very great importance the word " provincial " was held to cover everything municipal inasmuch as the provincial authority creates the municipality.

Very often the postmaster or the collector of customs occupies the position of reeve, or other office in a municipal council, and it would be a pity to deprive them of the enjoyment of that privilege.

Would this be considered partisanship:	A postmaster is a
road foreman under the provincial government. He has power to engage men and dismiss them as he likes, and I know of instances where he has exercised the power just as he fancied. Would that be called partisanship?
This section would not cover that case.

Would he not be using
party funds? As the schedule does not contain a definition of what " party funds " are I would like to know from the minister what is meant by the term?

I do not know,
perhaps my hon. friend; would undertake to give a definition.

Nobody in this House
could define what party funds are.

Let us be serious. I
consider that the last line of the first section advertises Canada in rather a wrong way. It smacks of corruption and I would drop the expressions used there.

"Party funds"
need not necessarily suggest corruption.
Generally it does.
Not always

Generally it does, from what I have seen in the case of others. I do not think it is a line that should be ai-lowed to remain there because you seem to say by this section: "You A, B and 0 in the Civil Service being electors and on the list can cast your vote. I, your chief or vour party leader, may receive and deal with any money or any party funds, but not you." It seems to me that we should not advertise in this way the political corruption that may take place in the country.

We will take another round out of this clause which reads:
No deputy head, officer, clerk or employee In the public service shall be debarred from voting at any Dominion or provincial election.
As a matter of fact I understand that in some of the provinces, Dominion civil servants are not permitted to vote at provincial elections. I think that is the case in the province of Ontario. It would seem as if this section confers upon such civil servant the right to vote in provincial elections which we have no power to do. As long as we say that they are not debarred from voting in the Dominion elections, that is as far as we can go. The section goes on to say:
If, under the laws governing the said, election, he has the right to vote; but no such deputy head, officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work.
-and so on. Now we have discussed what constituted partisan work in this House and we have had some very violent arguments about it. It was declared at that time that partisan work was not objectionable unless it was of an offensive character. The mere
fact that a man went around in the company of a few party friends smoking his pipe peacefully, or attended a political meeting, was not regarded as partisanship as long as he did not do anything offensive or act in a partisan way. But we are leaving the word "offensive" out altogether in this Bill, and a man who simply attended a political meeting would be considered guilty of an offence	as the Bill
stands. A member of the Civil ' Ser-who went to a political meeting and merely listened to the speakers, he would he regarded as having engaged in partisan work. I think the minister would be well advised if he inserted the word " offensive " in the section. That would give a man in the public service a chance to justify himself who happened to be in a crowd listening to a soap box orator who was delivering an arraignment against this Government, because that man could say, " I did not take any part in the proceedings. I was only an on-looker." The clause as it now stands is a very drastic one and could be construed in a very drastic manner. Under the old definition everybody -in the service knew what was meant; they could attend a political gathering and they could vote; tout they could not become agents or canvassers or take an offensive part in an election. That is only fair; I would not deprive any man in the service of the right to attend a political meeting. He has the right to vote and before voting should have the right to listen to both sides if he so desires. For that reason I would ask the minister to insert the word " offensive " before the words " partisan work." Hundreds of men. have been charged with violation of the law and taking part in elections offensively and it all hinged on whether they were offensive partisans or not.
Who shall decide whether a civil, servant has been engaged in political work such as to merit dismissal?
The judge.

If dismissal was a penalty I suppose the minister, the deputy head or the commission should decide that. I think it very important, now that the Civil Service Act is being made applicable to the Outside Service, that all public servants abstain from taking part in elections. They are, of course, entitled to the right of attending meetings and to vote.
You invite them under this clause to take part in politics. They are not debarred from voting at elections.

They have the right to vote but not to engage in partisan work. I mention this in the interest of the service-and I think it is also in the public interest-that hereafter they abstain from taking part in an election.
Who shall decide whether an officer has been offensively partisan and deserves dismissal? Will it be the minister, the deputy head or the commission?
The Governor in Council under section 30.
I would say the commission.

The word "active,'' if inserted in the section, would solve the problem. There is no harm in a man attending a political meeting, but if he goes out and canvasses, or does any work in the election on behalf of any candidate, or takes any part in organizing, he is an active partisan.

I object to the clause as it stands, because it is open to such wide interpretation. The Elections Act provides that a man taking part in an election must either be an agent or a canvasser, drive voters to the poll, and so on. All these things are clearly defined as taking a partisan part in an election. If we are providing a penalty of $500 or imprisonment, we should not leave the interpretation of political partisanship so wide open. If a public servant happens to stand on a street comer when a political meeting is taking place, he might be charged with partisan-iship, taken before a magistrate and fined $500. The wording of the clause is altogether too loose with a penalty so high as that, and in justice to these men it should be clearly stated what partisanship consists of, whether attending public meetings, speaking, canvassing for votes, driving voters to the polls, treating or entertaining them in any way.
There is no more treating.

[DOT] There is, in some parts of the country. Some definition should be included in this clause similar to that contained in the Elections Act. There are certain definitions in that Act of what "taking an active part in an election" is, and of what an "agent" is. But this section is open to any construction whatsoever.

I think the section is correct as it stands. I do not think any person in this House will have any diffi-

culty in deciding whether or not a man is taking a partisan part in an election. And I do not think you can make this provision too strict. I think that men appointed to positions in the public service should absolutely eschew partisan politics; they should not do any more than cast their ballot. That is what this clause gives them permission to do. I think we are splitting hairs. I do not think this section can be misunderstood by any person. And if any civil servant is in doubt as to its meaning, it is his business to be on the right side, and if he keeps on the right side he won't be fined $500.

Might I call attention to what I consider to be a somewhat drastic provision. We are all actuated by the desire to punish men on the opposite side of politics, and we are always prepared to condone anything our own friends do, and candidates always try to get everybody to do as much as possible on their behalf. This section provides that any person violating its provisions shall be tried summarily. But who is going to lay an information against an individual whereby he is going to be penalised and fined $500?
The other fellow.

Who is going to take the responsibility of seeing such a man go to jail and his wife and family suffering because he has been induced to do something which has been created a wrong by this section? Is it not sufficient to have that man dismissed)? Another objection to the clause is this, and I think some of the ministers in the House will confirm what I say. You proceed under summary conviction and go before a justice of the peace. Now I know how these gentlemen are appointed, and I am free to say that if there was a Conservative Administration in the province of Alberta they would probably dismiss every justice of the peace and put their own people in.
Why?
Because it is done in practice, the same as it is done in all the provinces of Canada.
That is a reflection on the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton).
The Minister of Customs would not do it himself personally.

It would be done by others more criminal still.

i
Mr. H. A. MAiCKIE: It may be more criminal. However, it is a fact, as the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) knows, that this practice pertains not only to the province of Alberta but also to the province of Quebec.
Oh, no.
Then I should like to live there and learn the political ethics of that fine province.
You would learn to put in more of your friends but not to dismiss the old ones.

I am not going into any vicious practices in Alberta. But from my experience there, the justices of the peace are all good politicians, and I fancy you would have to take appeals in all of these cases and go before the district court. I think the section is a little too drastic. And if the public servant does anything politically which he ought not to do, under this section, it seeme to m.e, that he has a fairly gocfd punishment if he is put out.
What is thq old law?
The old law had no sanction at all.
No penalty?
There is no penalty in the present Act.

I move that the words "be [DOT]guilty of an offence and liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding five. hundred dollars or imprisonment for [DOT]any period not exceeding one month and to" be struck out. Under the Elections Act a penalty is provided for certain offences. The fact that a man is a civil servant does not prevent his coming under that law, but here, because he is a civil servant, we make a further punishment. We all know that in an election feeling runs high. If I saw a civil servant running against me, while I might not personally say anything, my political friends will say: "I will have this fellow fined. " That is not fair.
Is dismissal sufficient? .

Certainly. I think it is
the only power we should exercise.

Why put impossible and
sumptuary legislation such as this on the statute books? We all know very well that when an election takes place in some quarters of the country feeling runs high and hot, and men have been taken and locked
up in jail, habeas corpus and everything else forgotten, simply because they have been found as strangers at a hotel. We should put an end to that kind of nonsense, and clearly define in this section what partisanship shall consist of. I would like the minister to have inserted after the words " shall engage in partisan work" the words-"such as canvassing, speaking" and so on, or put in the definition which is in the Elections Act as to what constitutes agency. In that way the public servant will know exactly what he can be convicted of.
